sections.heading: Advent of Europeans & the struggle for supremacy

blocks.text: European trade with India began with **Vasco da Gama at Calicut (1498)** and became a **century-long contest** among the **Portuguese, Dutch, English, French and Danes**. The **Anglo-French Carnatic Wars** decided that the **English East India Company** would win the race — turning trade into territorial empire.

rows: First; **Goa (1510, Albuquerque), Daman, Diu**; blue-water/cartaz policy; held Goa till 1961.
**Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta**; won via naval-financial strength.
Anglo-French; **Wandiwash (1760)** decisive; **Treaty of Paris (1763)** ended French ambitions.

items: Order of arrival: Portuguese→Dutch→English→French→Danes; da Gama 1498; Goa 1510 (Albuquerque).
Three Carnatic Wars; Wandiwash (1760) sealed English supremacy over the French.

prelimsPointers: **Vasco da Gama** reached **Calicut (1498)**; welcomed by the **Zamorin**.
**Portuguese** — **Alfonso de Albuquerque** captured **Goa (1510)**; Cartaz pass system; held Goa till **1961**.
**Dutch (VOC, 1602)**; **English EIC (1600)**; **French (CIO, 1664)**; **Danes (1616)**.
English factories — **Surat (1613), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta (1690)**.
**Carnatic Wars (three, 1746-63)** — Anglo-French; **Dupleix** (French) vs Clive.
**Battle of Wandiwash (1760)** — English decisively beat the French (Count de Lally).
**Treaty of Paris (1763)** ended French political ambitions in India.
mainsAngles: Why did the English succeed over other European powers in India?

glossary.definition: The Portuguese naval pass system compelling Indian ships to pay for trading rights.
Three Anglo-French conflicts (1746-63) that established English supremacy in south India.
The 1760 battle where the English decisively defeated the French in the Carnatic.

sections.heading: Regional focus — Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Mysore, Andhra, Nizam

blocks.text: The Company's rise was won region by region — **Bengal (Plassey, Buxar) gave the financial base; Mysore (four wars vs Hyder Ali & Tipu) and the Nizam of Hyderabad (Subsidiary Alliance)** anchored the south, with **coastal Andhra** (the Northern Circars) an early prize.

rows: **Plassey (1757)** — Clive vs Siraj-ud-Daulah; **Buxar (1764)** → **Diwani (1765)**; the empire's financial base.
**Four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-99)**; **Hyder Ali & Tipu Sultan**; Tipu died at **Seringapatam (1799)**.
First to accept **Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798)**; a loyal ally.
Ceded to the English (1765-66); coastal Andhra came under Company/Madras Presidency early.

items: Bengal (Plassey-Buxar-Diwani) = financial base; Mysore (Tipu, Seringapatam 1799); Nizam = first Subsidiary Alliance.
Northern Circars = coastal Andhra came under the English early (1760s).

prelimsPointers: **Plassey (1757)** — Clive defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah** (Mir Jafar's betrayal); **Buxar (1764)** → **Diwani (1765)**.
**Anglo-Mysore Wars** — **Hyder Ali & Tipu Sultan**; **Tipu killed at Seringapatam (1799)**; Tipu — 'Tiger of Mysore', rocketry.
**Nizam of Hyderabad** — first ruler to accept **Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798)**.
**Northern Circars** (coastal Andhra) ceded to the English (1765-66) — under Madras Presidency.
**Three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-1818)** ended Maratha power; **Three Anglo-Sikh** (later) annexed Punjab.
**Guntur Circar** was the last acquired (1788).
**Rani of Sivaganga, Velu Nachiyar** and Andhra poligars resisted early Company rule.
mainsAngles: Trace the Company's territorial expansion across Bengal, Mysore and the Deccan.

glossary.definition: The coastal-Andhra districts ceded to the English East India Company in the 1760s.
Wellesley's system whereby Indian rulers hosted Company troops at their own cost; the Nizam was first to accept.
Tipu Sultan's capital, where he died in 1799 ending the Anglo-Mysore Wars.

blocks.text: British India was administered by a line of **Governor-Generals (1773–1858)** and, after the Crown took over, **Viceroys (1858–1947)**, each associated with landmark **reforms, wars, annexations and movements** — a favourite exam matching set.

rows: First GG of Bengal; Regulating Act; Pitt's India Act; Asiatic Society (Jones).
**Permanent Settlement (1793)**; civil-service & judicial reforms ('father of civil service').
**Abolition of Sati (1829)**; English education (Macaulay 1835); suppressed thugee.
**Local self-government (1882)**; Ilbert Bill; repealed Vernacular Press Act.

items: Match reforms to officials: Cornwallis-Permanent Settlement, Bentinck-Sati, Dalhousie-railways/Lapse, Ripon-local self-govt, Curzon-Bengal partition.

prelimsPointers: **Warren Hastings** — first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773).
**Cornwallis** — **Permanent Settlement (1793)**; 'father of Indian Civil Service'.
**Bentinck** — abolished **Sati (1829)**; **Macaulay's Minute (1835)** English education.
**Dalhousie** — **Doctrine of Lapse**; started **railways & telegraph (1853)**; annexed Awadh (1856).
**Canning** — last GG, **first Viceroy** (post-1858); Revolt of 1857.
**Ripon** — **Local Self-Government (1882)**; Ilbert Bill; **Curzon** — **Partition of Bengal (1905)**, founded **ASI**.
**Minto II** (Morley-Minto 1909), **Chelmsford** (1919 Act), **Irwin** (Dandi/Gandhi-Irwin pact), **Mountbatten** (last Viceroy, Partition).
mainsAngles: Assess the reforms of the major Governor-Generals of British India.

glossary.definition: The head of British Indian administration (1773-1858); after 1858 the same office was styled Viceroy.
Dalhousie's policy of annexing princely states lacking a natural heir.
Cornwallis's 1793 revenue settlement fixing zamindars' land tax in perpetuity.

sections.heading: The Revolt of 1857 — origin, nature, causes & significance

blocks.text: The **Revolt of 1857** — India's **'First War of Independence'** — began as a **sepoy mutiny at Meerut (10 May 1857)** over the **greased cartridges** and swelled into a broad **civil-military uprising** against a century of British rule. Though suppressed, it ended Company rule and reshaped British policy.

rows: **Enfield rifle greased cartridges** (cow & pig fat); **Mangal Pandey** (Barrackpore, 29 March 1857).
**Political (Lapse, annexations), economic (drain, ruin of artisans/peasants), military (discrimination, service conditions), socio-religious (reforms, conversion fears)**.
**Bahadur Shah II (Delhi), Nana Saheb & Tantia Tope (Kanpur), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Kunwar Singh (Bihar)**.
By 1858; British recaptured Delhi; Bahadur Shah exiled to Rangoon.
**Government of India Act 1858** — Crown rule; end of the Company & Mughal line; Doctrine of Lapse dropped; army reorganised.

items: Immediate spark = greased cartridges; Mangal Pandey; Meerut 10 May 1857; centres & leaders.
Result = GoI Act 1858 (Crown rule). Nature debated: sepoy mutiny vs first war of independence (Savarkar).

prelimsPointers: Immediate cause — **greased cartridges** of the **Enfield rifle**; **Mangal Pandey** fired the first shot (Barrackpore).
Revolt broke out at **Meerut (10 May 1857)**; symbolic leader **Bahadur Shah II** (Delhi).
Leaders — **Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope (Kanpur); Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi); Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow); Kunwar Singh (Bihar)**.
Did NOT spread to the **south** & much of Bengal/Punjab; educated Indians & most princes stayed aloof.
**Government of India Act 1858** — abolished the Company; **Crown rule**; **Queen's Proclamation**.
**V.D. Savarkar** called it the **'First War of Independence'**; others term it a sepoy mutiny.
The **Doctrine of Lapse** was abandoned and the **army reorganised** (higher British ratio).
mainsAngles: Analyse the causes, nature and significance of the Revolt of 1857.

glossary.definition: Enfield-rifle cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, the immediate trigger of 1857.
The Act that ended Company rule and transferred India to direct Crown administration.
The sepoy at Barrackpore whose defiance in March 1857 presaged the revolt.
